sections.text: The COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, collapsed without a final overarching agreement after negotiations hit unbridgeable red lines over fossil fuels. A proposed compromise text failed to mention fossil fuels directly, prompting roughly two-thirds of attending countries, including EU member states, to reject it. Oil-producing nations opposed explicit phase-out language and climate finance terms, leading to the longest UN climate summit ending in deadlock.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The breakdown highlights deep geopolitical divisions and raises questions about the effectiveness of the consensus-based COP model. Critics and officials argued that allowing a small group of petrostates veto power over vital climate action undermines global progress. However, supporters noted that despite the summit's failure, renewable energy transitions continue to advance in the real world.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Arctic air swept across a large swathe of Europe, opening a corridor of cold air driven by high pressure over Scandinavia and low pressure shifting into western Russia. Extensive snowfall also occurred in regions including southern Poland, Belarus, Ukraine, and the Alps.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The cold spell in Europe contrasts starkly with global temperature trends, which continue to set records through a strong El Niño. Meanwhile, the significant dumping of snow provides a welcome boost for ski resorts in the Alps ahead of their upcoming openings.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: High pressure is set to remain dominant across northern Europe into the weekend and early December, maintaining below-average temperatures in central and eastern Europe and potentially extending into the Balkans. Cold easterly winds might also reach western Europe and the UK.
